title: Advanced Typing: Union, Optional, Any & Literal

slides.title: Union, Optional, Any, and Literal Types
slides.prompt: Python 3.10 introduced the `|` operator for union types. `Optional[T]` represents `T | None`. `Literal` restricts arguments to specific exact values, while `Any` disables type checking for a variable.

slides.title: Union Syntax Operator (Python 3.10+)
slides.prompt: Fill in the bitwise operator used as a shorthand for Union types in Python 3.10+.
slides.codeSnippet:
def parse(val: int ___ str) -> float:
    return float(val)

slides.title: Literal Type Hinting Import
slides.prompt: Fill in the class name imported from typing to constrain a argument to a fixed set of specific literal values.

slides.title: Consequences of Any Type
slides.prompt: What happens when a parameter is annotated with `typing.Any`?
options: Static type checkers allow any operation and skip type validation for that variable
It restricts the parameter to primitive types (int, float, str, bool)
Python automatically converts the passed argument into a string at runtime
The static type checker treats it as an object that has no methods
slides.correctAnswer: Static type checkers allow any operation and skip type validation for that variable

slides.title: NoReturn Type Usage
slides.prompt: When should `typing.NoReturn` be used as a function return annotation?
options: When a function never returns normally (e.g., raises an exception or runs an infinite loop)
When a function returns None explicitly
When a function has no return statement
When a function's return type cannot be inferred
slides.correctAnswer: When a function never returns normally (e.g., raises an exception or runs an infinite loop)
